title: Neural Networks
subtitle: Perceptrons, backpropagation, and deep learning with Keras

whyItExists.problem: Traditional ML algorithms require manual feature engineering and struggle with high-dimensional data like images, audio, and text. A cat in a photo cannot be described by a simple set of if-then rules.
whyItExists.solution: Neural networks learn hierarchical feature representations directly from raw data. Each layer learns progressively more abstract features — edges → shapes → faces → identity — without manual engineering.
whyItExists.whenToUse: For images, audio, text, and other high-dimensional data where manual feature engineering is impractical. Also when you have very large datasets (100k+ examples) where deep learning can exploit the data better than classical methods.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For tabular structured data — gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) almost always outperforms neural networks there. Also when data is scarce (< 10k examples) and interpretability is required.

explainModes.beginner: A neural network is inspired by the brain. It has layers of nodes (neurons). Data enters at the first layer, travels through hidden layers that transform it, and the final layer gives an answer. Training is like adjusting millions of dials until the network gets the right answers.
explainModes.simple: Each layer of a neural network applies a matrix multiplication (linear transform) followed by an activation function (non-linear squash). By stacking many layers, the network can learn very complex patterns. Training uses backpropagation to adjust all weights so predictions get better.
explainModes.standard: Neural networks stack layers: each computes z = Wx + b, then a = σ(z) where σ is a non-linear activation (ReLU, sigmoid, softmax). Training minimises a loss function via stochastic gradient descent. Backpropagation computes gradients via the chain rule.
explainModes.technical: A feedforward network is a composition of functions f(x) = f_L(f_{L-1}(...f_1(x))). Each layer applies an affine transform followed by a pointwise non-linearity. SGD with momentum (Adam) minimises the empirical loss. Backprop computes ∂L/∂w via the chain rule efficiently in O(n) time.
explainModes.deepDive: Universal approximation theorem: a 2-layer network with enough hidden units can approximate any continuous function. In practice, depth is preferred over width — it provides exponential representational efficiency. Modern training tricks: batch normalisation, residual connections, attention mechanisms, and self-supervised pretraining.

content.text: A neural network is a stack of layers, each applying a linear transformation followed by a non-linear activation function. The non-linearity is what allows deep networks to learn complex patterns that no linear model can capture.

content.definition: Every neuron connects to every neuron in the previous layer. Computes z = Wx + b (linear), then a = σ(z) (activation). The weights W and biases b are learned during training.
Rectified Linear Unit: f(x) = max(0, x). The most common hidden-layer activation. Fast to compute, avoids the vanishing gradient problem that plagued earlier sigmoids.
The algorithm that computes gradients of the loss with respect to every weight in the network using the chain rule. These gradients tell the optimiser how to adjust each weight to reduce loss.

content.text: Building a Binary Classifier with Keras

content.code:
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import numpy as np

# Scale data (critical for neural networks)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_sc = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_sc  = scaler.transform(X_test)
X_val_sc   = scaler.transform(X_val)

# Build model
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Input(shape=(X_train.shape[1],)),
    keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu'),
    keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
    keras.layers.Dropout(0.3),          # randomly zero 30% of neurons during training
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu'),
    keras.layers.Dropout(0.2),
    keras.layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')  # binary classification → probability
])

model.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
    loss='binary_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy', keras.metrics.AUC(name='auc')]
)

model.summary()

callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
        monitor='val_loss',
        patience=10,           # stop if no improvement for 10 epochs
        restore_best_weights=True  # keep the best model, not the last
    ),
    keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(
        monitor='val_loss',
        factor=0.5,            # halve learning rate on plateau
        patience=5
    )
]

history = model.fit(
    X_train_sc, y_train,
    epochs=200,
    batch_size=64,
    validation_data=(X_val_sc, y_val),
    callbacks=callbacks,
    verbose=1
)

# Evaluate
loss, acc, auc = model.evaluate(X_test_sc, y_test)
print(f'Test accuracy: {acc:.3f}  AUC: {auc:.3f}')

# Probabilities for precision/recall analysis
probs = model.predict(X_test_sc).flatten()

# For N classes, change the final layer and loss
n_classes = 10

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Input(shape=(784,)),          # e.g., MNIST 28x28 flattened
    keras.layers.Dense(256, activation='relu'),
    keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
    keras.layers.Dropout(0.4),
    keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu'),
    keras.layers.Dropout(0.3),
    keras.layers.Dense(n_classes, activation='softmax')  # outputs N probabilities summing to 1
])

model.compile(
    optimizer='adam',
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',  # use when labels are integers
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

# Or use 'categorical_crossentropy' if labels are one-hot encoded

content.text: Dropout randomly sets a fraction of neurons to zero during each training step. This forces the network to not rely on any single neuron, acting as an ensemble of many smaller networks. It is the standard regularisation technique for neural networks.

content.title: Neural Networks vs Gradient Boosting (Tabular Data)

a.name: Neural Networks (Keras/PyTorch)
a.description: Learns representations through stacked differentiable layers
weaknesses: Usually worse than GBT on tabular data
Requires much more data and tuning
Slow to train, hard to interpret
a.useWhen: Images, audio, text, sequences, very large datasets (100k+)

b.name: XGBoost / LightGBM
weaknesses: Requires feature engineering for temporal data
b.useWhen: Structured / tabular data, most real-world business datasets

content.text: Use EarlyStopping(restore_best_weights=True) to automatically save the best checkpoint during training. Without this, you get the final weights which are usually worse than the best validation checkpoint.
Always scale inputs before feeding them to a neural network. Without scaling, gradients for different features will have wildly different magnitudes, making training slow and unstable.

questions.question: What does backpropagation do?
options: Feeds data forward through the network to compute predictions
Computes gradients of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule
Regularises the model by zeroing neurons randomly
Initialises weights with small random values
questions.explanation: Backpropagation efficiently computes ∂Loss/∂w for every weight in the network using the chain rule, working backwards from the loss to the input layer.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Dropout in a neural network?
options: To speed up training by using fewer neurons
To prevent overfitting by randomly zeroing neurons during training
To initialise weights closer to zero
questions.explanation: Dropout is a regularisation technique that randomly sets a fraction of neurons to zero during each training step, preventing co-adaptation and reducing overfitting.

questions.question: Which activation function should be used in the final layer for binary classification?
questions.explanation: Sigmoid maps any value to (0, 1), making it ideal for binary classification where you want a probability. Use softmax for multi-class and linear (no activation) for regression.

faq.q: Should I use neural networks or gradient boosting for tabular data?
faq.a: Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) usually outperforms neural networks on tabular/structured data. Use neural networks for images, text, and audio — data where feature learning from raw inputs is the core challenge.

faq.q: How many layers and neurons should I use?
faq.a: Start small (2 hidden layers, 64-128 neurons each) and add complexity only if the validation score keeps improving. More capacity is not always better — it increases overfitting risk and training time.

faq.q: What is the difference between batch size and epochs?
faq.a: An epoch is one full pass through the training data. Batch size is how many samples are processed before updating weights. Smaller batches (32-64) introduce more noise (can help generalisation). Larger batches are more stable but need more memory.
